statement: Seven whole numbers are written around a circle. For each pair of neighbours, Pia adds the two numbers together, which gives seven sums. At most how many of the seven sums can be odd?

choices.misconception: I split the seven numbers into separate pairs of neighbours, which only gives 3 pairs, but every number belongs to two neighbouring pairs.
I paired each odd number with just one neighbour, so with 4 odd and 3 even numbers I counted only 4 odd sums.
I alternated odd and even around the circle and thought the place where the pattern breaks spoils the pair on each side of it.
I alternated odd and even all the way round, not noticing that with seven numbers the first and last are both odd and sit next to each other.

hints: When is the sum of two numbers odd?
A sum is odd exactly when one number is odd and the other is even. Walk round the circle and count how many times you switch between odd and even. You must end where you started.
Going all the way round brings you back to the number you started from, so the number of switches is even. It cannot be 7.

solutions.reliable: A sum of two neighbours is odd exactly when one is odd and the other is even, that is, wherever you switch between odd and even as you walk round the circle. Walking all the way round brings you back to the starting number, so you switch an even number of times. So at most 6 of the 7 sums are odd. Six is possible: the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in order around the circle give the sums 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 8, and only 8 is even. The transferable idea: going round a closed loop, the number of switches between two states is always even.
solutions.elegant: Add up all seven sums. Each number is used in two sums, so the total is twice the sum of the numbers, which is even. Seven odd sums would add up to an odd total, so at least one sum must be even. The example 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 shows that 6 odd sums can happen.

whyOnTest: Parity arguments show what is impossible: around a circle of odd length, odd and even numbers cannot alternate all the way round.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
